page: Google Cloud Platform e2-highcpu-2 is an entry-level compute-focused instance within the E2 family. It features 2 virtual CPUs powered by an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor operating at 2.2 GHz, backed by 1 physical core with 2 threads per core under dedicated CPU allocation. The server includes 2.0 GB of system memory, providing a 1.0 GB per vCPU ratio, with no bundled local SSD storage or attached GPU accelerators.

Performance benchmarks indicate entry-tier baseline capabilities. Synthetic CPU testing yields a stress-ng single-core score of 1105.98 and a multi-core score of 1452.89, alongside a Geekbench multi-core score of 1073.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 1664.25. Uncached memory write bandwidth sits at 11.11 GB/sec, while static web serving throughput measures 1.39 GB/sec. These scores reflect modest multi-threading and memory bandwidth constraints suited primarily for light execution overhead.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the instance offers an economical hardware profile for small-scale workloads where low memory overhead is acceptable. Due to its limited 2.0 GB memory capacity and baseline CPU throughput, the instance is appropriate for lightweight microservices, basic web serving, simple utility scripts, or modest development and testing tasks.
description: Google Cloud Platform e2-highcpu-2 is a budget-focused compute-oriented instance powered by a 2.2 GHz Intel Xeon x86_64 processor. Configured with 2 vCPUs across 1 physical core with multithreading, it delivers 2.0 GB of RAM (1.0 GB per vCPU) with no attached local storage or GPU hardware. In benchmark testing, the server demonstrates entry-level performance, achieving a PassMark CPU score of 1664.25, a Geekbench multi-core score of 1073.0, and static web serving throughput of 1.39 GB/sec. Memory read and write bandwidths reach 13.03 GB/sec and 11.11 GB/sec respectively. Given its tight 2.0 GB RAM overhead and moderate processing ceiling, e2-highcpu-2 provides a cost-effective environment for low-concurrency web hosting, lightweight background microservices, basic utility automation, and early-stage software testing workloads where resource demands remain low.
